newsitem.title: ITALY: WFP head says Zaire force must control militants.
newsitem.headline: WFP head says Zaire force must control militants.

text.p: The head of the U.N.'s food aid arm said on Thursday that an international force for eastern Zaire must separate "the bad guys with the guns" from starving refugees or its mission would have to be repeated.

Catherine Bertini, executive director of the World Food Programme (WFP), also said that while the first step would be seeing that no weapons interfered with humanitarian work, ultimately fighters would have to be disarmed.
Bertini said the situation in eastern Zaire had become horrific. The agency assumed that many people were now surviving on roots, leaves and fruit.
"I think the first step is separating people, not necessarily disarming people," Bertini told reporters at the U.N.-sponsored World Food Summit in Rome.

"The step necessary for peace in the long term is disarmament but if we're talking about keeping people alive and feeding people today we would want to separate the bad guys with the guns from the people who need to live today," she said.
President Bill Clinton has tentatively agreed to order U.S. troops to help the rescue of Rwandan and Burundian Hutus, some cut off from help since Zairean Tutsis rebelled a month ago.
White House press secretary Mike McCurry said Washington believed the mission would have to be clearly defined and not try to disarm militants or conduct any kind of forced entry.

Bertini, asked if her comments put her at odds with Washington's position, said she had to defer to military experts on how the mission should be carried out but stressed that people with weapons would have to be kept far from the refugees.

"We must rely on a major effort on the part of the multinational intervention force so that we don't return to the status quo, so that we don't return to refugees in camps controlled by intimidators with guns," she said.

"I don't think anybody wants to see a repeat of what has happened already. If we just recreate the camps and have the camps operate exactly the same way...then this multinational force is going to have to come back in a year to re-do it again because it'll start with the same problem all over again."

The difficulties facing the force were underscored on Thursday as heavy fighting flared around the eastern town of Goma between rebels and their Hutu foes holed up in the teeming refugee camp of Mugunga.
Bertini said the only weapons that should be tolerated were those protecting aid workers.
She said that before the crisis the refugees were receiving 70 percent of food needs from humanitarian programmes.
"So now, we can only guess as to how these people are surviving -- on roots, on leaves, on fruit, on anything they might find," she said.

Bertini told the summit's plenary session on Wednesday night her agency estimated that within a month 80,000 children would die, 50,000 more children would suffer severe malnutrition and 75,000 more people would succumb to dysentery and cholera.
She said the agency would be asking the international community to pledge a further $136 million in food aid because of the crisis.
